title: Oxygen Absorbers: What the cc Number Means
description: cc is oxygen capacity, not food capacity. How to size by air volume, where the manufacturer charts disagree, and why vacuum sealing is not oxygen-free.

howTo.name: Find the container's total volume
howTo.text: Use the container's own figure in millilitres or cubic centimetres. One millilitre equals one cubic centimetre, and one gallon is 3,785cc of air [6][7]. Impak publishes reference volumes: a #10 can is 3,980cc, a five-gallon plastic pail is 18,942cc, a six-gallon pail is 22,730.4cc [2].

howTo.name: Subtract the food, keep the void space
howTo.text: Impak's worked example takes an 18,942cc pail, subtracts 15,876g of rice, and is left with 3,066cc of residual air - the headspace plus the gaps between grains [2]. PackFreshUSA notes those gaps do not shrink with particle size: 'A pool filled with marbles will have the same interstitial air volume as one filled with basketballs' [6].

howTo.name: Multiply by the oxygen fraction
howTo.text: Impak multiplies residual air by 0.21: '3,066 (cc) residual air volume x .21 (oxygen fraction in air) = 628.53 cc oxygen' [2]. Published oxygen fractions across the manufacturers in this scan run 21.0%, 21%, 20.95%, 20.5% and 20% [2][6][8][5][9], so the result is an estimate, not a constant.

howTo.name: Round up to the next stocked size
howTo.text: Impak's 628.53cc calculation is rounded to a 750cc packet [2]. Four suppliers state that excess capacity does no harm: 'Excess absorbers are harmless - they simply won't fully react' [8]; 'There is no danger in adding too many as this does not affect the food' [1][6][7].

faq.question: What does the cc number on an oxygen absorber mean?
faq.answer: It is the packet's oxygen-absorbing capacity in cubic centimetres, not a food quantity. Dry & Dry states the rating 'corresponds to the amount of oxygen absorbed' [1]; Utah State Extension defines cc as 'cubic centimeters as it relates to amount of oxygen absorbing capacity' [3]. PackFreshUSA puts the distinction directly: the rating tells you 'how much oxygen the absorber can remove, not how much food it protects' [4]. Impak treats the number as a floor - a 500cc packet should absorb a minimum of 500cc [5].

faq.question: What size absorber does a one-gallon bag of freeze-dried food need?
faq.answer: The published answers for a one-gallon container range from 100cc to 800cc across nine sources [9][12][8][15][3][7][14][1][17][6]. For bulky, high-air-volume contents specifically, two sources publish a figure: PackFreshUSA places freeze-dried food in a 75%-air class and says 'Using a 500cc in a gallon container would ensure you would remove all the oxygen' [12], and Discount Mylar Bags lists 'bulky/freeze-dried = 500cc' for one gallon, conditioned on food below 10% moisture [8]. No manufacturer in this scan publishes a figure for a specific freeze-dried food such as berries.

faq.question: Can I use two small absorbers instead of one large one?
faq.answer: Manufacturers split on this. PackFreshUSA advises 'use one slightly larger absorber - not doubling up' [4] and Wallaby says 'Drop one absorber into each bag right before sealing' [11]. Against that, Oxygen-Absorbers.com says 'For bags over 5 kg, consider using two smaller absorbers to ensure even oxygen removal' [18], OxyFree offers 7 x 300cc as an alternative to one 2000cc packet [15], and Wallaby's own chart is expressed as counts of 100cc packets [7]. No source in this scan publishes a mechanism for the one-packet rule.

faq.question: Should the bag suck down if the absorber is working?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Absorbers remove only the oxygen fraction, so PackFreshUSA states '1/5 of the air volume will be gone but 4/5 of the air will always remain' [25], and 'You may not always see that vacuum-packed look even though the oxygen has indeed been removed' [25]. Wallaby names the belief as an error: 'It's a misconception that a vacuum-packed look confirms the oxygen has been removed' [26]. Discount Mylar Bags adds that powders and some freeze-dried loads may not contract at all [8].

faq.question: How long can absorbers sit out before they are spent?
faq.answer: Published working windows vary by an order of magnitude: 10 minutes [19], 10-15 minutes [14], 10-20 minutes [8], 15 minutes [3], 15-30 minutes [1], 30 minutes [18], and up to 90 minutes for a slow-acting product [16]. Harvest Right gives no number, only 'Once opened, oxygen absorbers begin working immediately' [17]. Dry & Dry states saturation takes 2-4 hours while still recommending 15-30 minutes [1]. Work to the shortest window your supplier publishes.

bodyHtml:
The short version: The cc number on an oxygen absorber is its oxygen-absorbing capacity in cubic centimetres, not a measure of how much food it covers [1][3][4]. You size it against the air left in the sealed container, not the weight of what you put in [10][11]. Use one packet sized up rather than two packets combined, and expect the published charts to disagree with each other by a wide margin.

What cc measures

Impak states the unit plainly: "Oxygen is measured in cubic centimeters (cc)" [2]. Utah State University Extension defines it as "cubic centimeters as it relates to amount of oxygen absorbing capacity" [3]. Dry & Dry says the size "corresponds to the amount of oxygen absorbed" [1].

Three things follow from that definition, and each one is stated by a manufacturer rather than inferred:

  • The number is about oxygen, not food. PackFreshUSA: the cc rating is "how much oxygen the absorber can remove, not how much food it protects" [4].
  • The number is a floor. Impak treats the rating as a minimum - a 500cc packet should absorb at least 500cc [5]. PackFreshUSA claims its high-capacity packets absorb "180% - 300% of their rating" [30]; OxyFree claims 300cc units measured "1106cc of actual absorption" [16]; AGM says O-Buster packets "pick up approximately three times their weight in oxygen" [9]. Those three claims use three different units and cannot be compared to each other.
  • The unit converts cleanly. Wallaby: "1 cc = 1 ml; 1000ml = 1 Liter; 3.78 Liters = 1 gallon" [7]. PackFreshUSA: "oxygen, as a gas, is measured in cc's, and containers are typically measured in milliliters, (ml) but conveniently, 1 ml = 1 cc" [6].

One counter-current exists. Impak alleges that some suppliers label packets by the total air volume they will treat rather than by oxygen capacity, so that "what is a 500cc packet is actually a 100cc packet" - its own testing of one supplier's S-100 units returned roughly 300cc [5]. If a chart's numbers look five times larger than everyone else's, that labelling convention is one explanation.

Why air volume, not food weight

Impak's worked five-gallon example is the clearest published arithmetic in the set: an 18,942cc pail holding 15,876g of rice leaves 3,066cc of residual air, and "3,066 (cc) residual air volume x .21 (oxygen fraction in air) = 628.53 cc oxygen" - rounded up to a 750cc packet [2].

The rule the arithmetic encodes is stated by three separate suppliers. Impak: "The size of oxygen absorber you need depends on the volume of air in the package into which it is placed" [10]. Wallaby: "Each bag size holds a different amount of air, so the absorber must match that volume" [11]. Wallaby again, on why weight fails: sizing must use "the container's residual air volume" [29].

Two complications sit inside that residual figure.

Void space counts, and particle size does not change it. Impak counts "the spaces in between" the product alongside the headspace [2]. PackFreshUSA's version is the most quoted line in the category: "A pool filled with marbles will have the same interstitial air volume as one filled with basketballs" [6]. That holds for identically shaped, similarly packed particles; freeze-dried food is neither uniform nor rigid, and mixed particle sizes let small pieces fill the gaps between large ones.

Different foods hold different fractions of air. PackFreshUSA publishes a three-class scheme: beans and rice "only have about 35% air volume", flour is about 50%, and freeze-dried, oats and pasta sit around 75% [12][19]. It applies the scheme to its own gallon figure - an empty gallon needs 800cc, but "if you were to fill the container with flour (which is about 50% air) then there should be 400cc's of oxygen in the filled gallon container" [6]. This is the only source in the scan that publishes an explicit freeze-dried percentage.

One source dissents from the whole method. Oxygen-Absorbers.com sizes by food weight - 1 kg of rice to 100cc, 2-3 kg to 200cc, 5 kg to 500cc, 10 kg to 1000cc - with no container volume in the calculation at all [18]. PackFreshUSA's "not how much food it protects" line is a direct rebuttal of that method [4].

The multiplier itself is not settled either. Published oxygen fractions of air across this scan are 21.0% [2], 21% [6][8][12], about 20.95% [8], 20.5% [5] and 20% [9]. Two suppliers contradict themselves across their own documents.

The sizing table

Every cell below is that source's own published number for that container. A blank means the source publishes nothing for it. Read across a row before you read down a column.

Impak also publishes a chart indexed by flat bag dimension rather than container: 20cc / 50cc for a 6" x 6" bag, 50cc / 100cc at 8" x 8", 100cc / 200cc at 10" x 14", 150cc / 300cc at 10" x 16", 500cc / 1000cc at 16" x 18", 750cc / 1500cc at 18" x 28" and 20" x 24", and 1000cc / 2000cc at 20" x 30" [13]. Its two columns are "Fine Grains (sugar, flour, etc.)" and "Pasta and Thicker, less Dense Foods" - it publishes no freeze-dried class [13].

Where they disagree, and why the spread is not noise:

  • One gallon spans 8x. 100cc [9] to 800cc [6]. PackFreshUSA explicitly labels the 300cc answer a myth [12], while USU Extension [3], O-Busters [9], Discount Mylar [8] and OxyFree [15] all publish exactly that number.
  • Five gallons spans 67% between two of the more careful sources alone. USU Extension publishes 1500cc [3]; Dry & Dry publishes 2500cc [1]. Impak's 750cc is not a container rating at all - it is conditioned on 35 lb of rice already occupying the pail [2], and comparing it to a 2000cc bucket recommendation is an error.
  • One quart splits a single supplier internally. PackFreshUSA's own math says 200cc, its own product ships 300cc, and it reconciles the two by stating that "200cc worth of oxygen absorbers are actually enough for a quart container, but as our quart bags can hold more than a quart, we use 300ccs in our Mylar sets" [6]. Nominal bag labels are not measured internal volumes.
  • Harvest Right's 700cc is the outlier with the thinnest condition. The only qualifier published is "For use in gallon-size Mylar bags" - no food class, no fill level [17] - and it comes from the dominant home freeze-dryer OEM.
  • The columns are not the same variable. O-Busters indexes by void-space percentage, not food type, and publishes only "under 10%" and "25% or more" - there is no middle band to interpolate [9]. Impak and Wallaby index by food density [13][7]. PackFreshUSA indexes by air-volume class [12].

Two of these sources disclaim their own charts. Impak: "This Chart represents approximate cc sizes and should not be taken as a final authority" [13]. Wallaby: the chart holds "only the average amount of oxygen absorbers needed" and "you may need more or a smaller number" [7]. No source in this scan presents its chart as authoritative, and a single canonical chart would contradict all of them.

One, never two

The practice statements are consistent. Wallaby: "Drop one absorber into each bag right before sealing" [11]. PackFreshUSA: "If you're unsure, use one slightly larger absorber - not doubling up" [4]. Discount Mylar directs one 2000cc packet into a five-gallon bucket rather than splitting the load [8].

What no manufacturer in this scan publishes is a reason. The rule appears only as practice; searches for a stated mechanism returned nothing. And three sources go the other way: Oxygen-Absorbers.com says "For bags over 5 kg, consider using two smaller absorbers to ensure even oxygen removal" [18]; PackFreshUSA elsewhere suggests buying 100cc or 200cc packets because "These are more easily used and add more as needed" [12]; Wallaby's own bucket chart is expressed as 20 to 30 packets of 100cc [7]. Both PackFreshUSA and Wallaby therefore contradict themselves between documents.

What is not in dispute is the direction of the error to make. Four sources state that surplus capacity is harmless: "Not only is it okay to use more absorbing power than necessary, it is a great idea" [6]; "There is no disadvantage to adding a greater number of oxygen absorbers packets than needed. It won't spoil your food" [7]; "Excess absorbers are harmless - they simply won't fully react" [8]; "There is no danger in adding too many as this does not affect the food" [1]. Undersizing has no equivalent safety margin.

One boundary applies to all of it: absorbers are for dry goods. Wallaby states that foods above 10% moisture, such as brown rice and beef jerky, do not benefit [29], and Discount Mylar's calculations assume food below 10% moisture [8].

Handling and the indicator

Absorbers begin working on contact with air, and the published working window varies by an order of magnitude: 10 minutes [19], 10-15 minutes [14], 10-20 minutes [8], 15 minutes [3], 15-30 minutes [1], 30 minutes [18], 20 minutes to start with ruin in as little as 5 hours [19], and up to 90 minutes for a slow-acting product [16]. Harvest Right publishes no number at all - only "Once opened, oxygen absorbers begin working immediately" [17]. Dry & Dry says saturation takes 2-4 hours while still recommending a 15-30 minute window [1], contradicting its own stated physics.

Two packaging formats exist to shorten the exposure rather than the clock. PackFreshUSA sells individually sealed packets so you can "open one at a time, reducing exposure, waste and the need to reseal" [30], and compartment packs of 5 or 10 [21]. Wallaby packages "in sets of ten to preserve effectiveness until use" [14]. For loose packets, PackFreshUSA's instruction is that "Unused oxygen absorbers may be stored in a mason jar or vacuum sealed" [6].

The colour indicator is less definitive than it looks:

ObservationPublished meaningSource
Pink or redOxygen removed, absorber good[21][19]
Blue or dark blueOxygen present[19][21]
Pink to blue transitionAgeless Eye changes pink to blue when oxygen is present; returns to pink as oxygen falls[22]
PurpleOxygen remains[5]
PurpleBenign transit state; indicators "will sometimes take over a week to become pink"[20]
Brown and clumpedSpent, versus "a fresh pink or gray powder"[3]

Purple carries two incompatible meanings across sources [5][20]. PackFreshUSA's own position is that the indicator is not the better test - a live absorber should "feel like fine powder" rather than hard and crunchy [20].

As for the end state, published residual oxygen figures are 0.1% or lower from Mitsubishi Gas Chemical [23], approximately 0.01% from Impak [27], and below 0.01% from PackFreshUSA [21] and Harvest Right [17]. The company that originated the technology publishes the least aggressive number.

Vacuum sealing is not oxygen-free

A vacuum sealer reduces the volume of gas in the bag. It does not change what that gas is made of - the residual is still about a fifth oxygen. PackFreshUSA states it directly: "Air still contains oxygen - even after vacuuming" [4]. Wallaby reframes the step as preparation rather than treatment: "This is not vacuum sealing; you're simply removing large pockets so the absorber will have less work to do" [11].

BeliefWhat manufacturers publishSource
Absorbers remove the air"Oxygen absorbers do not absorb air; they absorb oxygen, which is 21% of air."[24]
Absorbers pull a vacuum"1/5 of the air volume will be gone but 4/5 of the air will always remain."[25]
Suck-down proves the seal"You may not always see that vacuum-packed look even though the oxygen has indeed been removed."[25]
Suck-down proves the seal (2)"It's a misconception that a vacuum-packed look confirms the oxygen has been removed."[26]

Vacuum and absorber are equivalent (2)Absorbers bring levels "down to 0.01% or less" inside airtight mylar[26]
Low oxygen means safe"This low-oxygen environment is just right for the development of several pathogens, but one to be specifically concerned about is botulism."[28]

NC State Extension is the source to read twice on that last row. Reduced-oxygen packaging is pathogen-selective, not sterile, and "these disease-causing bacteria may not change the color or look of the food" [28]. Sealing does not reclassify a food: "Perishable foods that need to be refrigerated or frozen without vacuum packaging still need to be refrigerated or frozen once sealed" [28], and "vacuum packaging is not a substitution for the heat processing of home canned foods" [28]. Discount Mylar states the same boundary from the supply side - absorbers are for dry goods [8].

What we could not source

  • A cc figure for freeze-dried berries, or any specific freeze-dried food. No manufacturer in this scan publishes one. The closest published structures are PackFreshUSA's 75%-air class [12] and Discount Mylar's "bulky/freeze-dried = 500cc" per gallon [8].
  • A freeze-dried class in most sizing charts. Impak's chart stops at "Pasta and Thicker, less Dense Foods" [13]; Wallaby's stops at "Less Dense Foods (beans, pasta)" [7]; O-Busters has no food classes at all [9]. Harvest Right, a freeze-dryer OEM, publishes no freeze-dried-specific cc [17].
  • Any mechanism behind the one-absorber rule. Repeated searches for a manufacturer explaining why packets should not be split returned practice statements only [11][4] - no stated reason.
  • A 20.9% oxygen figure. No manufacturer in this scan publishes it. The published values are 21%, 21.0%, 20.95%, 20.5% and 20% [2][6][8][5][9].
  • Any exposure-time figure from Impak / Sorbent Systems, the most technically detailed supplier in the set. None appears in any document retrieved [2][5][13].
  • A regulator document naming oxygen absorber packets. A GRAS claim exists as a manufacturer assertion [19]; searching for a corresponding FDA document returned nothing, so we do not repeat the claim as established.
  • An oxygen-concentration threshold for the Ageless Eye colour change. Mitsubishi publishes the colour direction but no percentage [22].
  • Cc capacities from Multisorb or the English-language Mitsubishi Ageless pages. Type names and applications are published; capacities and selection math are not [23].
  • Non-ferrous absorbers above 100cc. The maximum published non-ferrous size is 100cc, so gallon and bucket volumes have no non-iron option in this scan [27].
  • Peer-reviewed literature on absorber performance. The one review located was inaccessible, so no independent test evidence sits behind any capacity claim here.
  • Measured internal volumes for common mylar bag sizes. PackFreshUSA's admission that its quart bags hold more than a quart [6] implies nominal labels are unreliable across the category, and nobody publishes measured figures.

Sublime Pantry has not bench-tested any absorber, bag, or food. Everything above is what the manufacturers and extension services publish, with their disagreements left visible rather than averaged away.
